context: All sequences run from front to rear. In this figure, push adds an element at the rear and pop removes and returns the front element.
description: Dashed squares show where elements were before an operation. They do not count as additional elements in the queue. A solid square moved outside the container shows the value returned by that pop.

steps.announcement: The initial queue is [1, 3, 2], with 1 at the front and 2 at the rear.
steps.explanation: The queue starts with three elements, [1, 3, 2] from front to rear. The front is 1 and the rear is 2. There is no return value.
steps.key_state: Initially, the queue is [1, 3, 2] from front to rear, with 1 at the front and 2 at the rear. There is no return value.
steps.title: Initial state

steps.announcement: Enqueue 5. The new rear element is 5.
steps.explanation: The call push(5) adds 5 at the rear. The existing elements keep their order. The queue now has four elements, [1, 3, 2, 5] from front to rear, with 1 at the front and 5 at the rear. The call returns no value.
steps.key_state: After push(5), the queue is [1, 3, 2, 5] from front to rear, with 1 at the front and 5 at the rear. There is no return value.
steps.title: push(5)

steps.announcement: Enqueue 4. The new rear element is 4.
steps.explanation: The call push(4) adds 4 at the rear, just after 5. The queue now has five elements, [1, 3, 2, 5, 4] from front to rear, with 1 at the front and 4 at the rear. The call returns no value.
steps.key_state: After push(4), the queue is [1, 3, 2, 5, 4] from front to rear, with 1 at the front and 4 at the rear. There is no return value.
steps.title: push(4)

steps.announcement: Remove and return 1 from the front. The new front is 3.
steps.explanation: The first call to pop() removes and returns the front element, 1. Its successor, 3, becomes the new front. The queue now has four elements, [3, 2, 5, 4] from front to rear, with 3 at the front and 4 at the rear. The returned 1 is outside the queue.
steps.key_state: After the first pop(), the queue is [3, 2, 5, 4] from front to rear, with 3 at the front and 4 at the rear. The call returns 1.
steps.title: First pop()

steps.announcement: Remove and return 3 from the front. The remaining queue is [2, 5, 4].
steps.explanation: The second call to pop() removes and returns the front element, 3, making 2 the new front. The queue now has three elements, [2, 5, 4] from front to rear, with 2 at the front and 4 at the rear. The returned 3 is outside the queue.
steps.key_state: After the second pop(), the queue is [2, 5, 4] from front to rear, with 2 at the front and 4 at the rear. The call returns 3.
steps.title: Second pop()

prose.summary: Elements enter at the rear and leave from the front, following the first-in, first-out rule.
prose.title: Enqueueing and dequeueing

context: All sequences run from front to rear. In this figure, push adds an element at the rear and pop removes and returns the front element.
description: Arrows connect five vertical panels from left to right, one for each row of the table below. In each panel, the front of the queue is at the top and the rear is at the bottom. Enqueue arrows enter from below, and dequeue arrows leave through the top.
Dashed squares show where elements were before an operation. They do not count as additional elements in the queue. A solid square moved outside the container shows the value returned by that pop.

frames.explanation: New elements can join only at the rear, so the existing elements keep their order. Even after 5 and 4 join the queue, two successive removals still return the original front element, 1, and then 3. This is first in, first out.
frames.title: Enqueueing and dequeueing
